explanations.explanation: Noah is the last name in that first run of verses: "Enoch, Methuselah, Lamech, Noah." (1 Chronicles 1:3) He's the man who went into the ark (Genesis 7:7). Ten names in three verses, friend, and the book never slows down to chat. I respect that kind of confidence.

Enoch is on the list, right at the start of verse 3, so you were in the right neighborhood. But he's not the last name in the run. The list keeps going: "Enoch, Methuselah, Lamech, Noah." (1 Chronicles 1:3) Noah is the one who went into the ark (Genesis 7:7), so he's the one at the end.

Methuselah is on the list, second in that line of four names. He's not the one at the end, though. After him come Lamech and then Noah (1 Chronicles 1:3). Noah is the man who went into the ark (Genesis 7:7). You were two names early, which on a list this long is basically a rounding error.

That's it. "The sons of Noah: Shem, Ham, and Japheth." (1 Chronicles 1:4) Three sons, and from here the whole list branches out like a family reunion that keeps getting bigger. Japheth is the one who comes third.

Lamech is a name from the verse before. He's listed in verse 3, just before Noah. The verse about Noah's sons says: "Shem, Ham, and Japheth." (1 Chronicles 1:4) So the blank is Japheth. Easy to mix up when the names come at you this fast, friend.

Enosh is way up at the top of the list, back in verse 1 with Adam and Seth. That makes him a distant ancestor of Noah, not one of his sons. The verse says: "The sons of Noah: Shem, Ham, and Japheth." (1 Chronicles 1:4) So Japheth fills the blank. Enosh is a great guess for the wrong century.

Yes! The line from Shem ends with "Abram (that is, Abraham)." (1 Chronicles 1:27) Same man, and the verse says so itself. After all those names you can't pronounce, a familiar one feels like spotting a friend in a crowded room.

Moses, Israel's leader, is a big name, but he isn't in this stretch of the list. The line from Shem lands on "Abram (that is, Abraham)." (1 Chronicles 1:27) Abraham is the one the names have been walking toward. Moses will have to wait his turn, friend.

David, Israel's king, is a famous name, but the list hasn't gotten anywhere near him yet. The line from Shem lands on "Abram (that is, Abraham)." (1 Chronicles 1:27) The verse even tells you Abram and Abraham are one man. David is a long way down the road.
That's right. "The sons of Abraham were Isaac and Ishmael." (1 Chronicles 1:28) The book gives it in one short line and moves on. Both of them get their own family lists coming up.

Isaac is right, but Peleg is way back in the family of Eber, a few generations before Abraham (1 Chronicles 1:19). So he can't be Abraham's son. The verse says: "The sons of Abraham were Isaac and Ishmael." (1 Chronicles 1:28) Half right, friend, and that's half a batch ready.

Isaac is right, but Terah is on the other side of Abraham. Terah comes just before him in the list (1 Chronicles 1:26), so he's the one in line before Abraham, not after. The verse says: "The sons of Abraham were Isaac and Ishmael." (1 Chronicles 1:28) Mixing up who comes before and after is easy on a list like this.

You got it. "Abraham was the father of Isaac. The sons of Isaac: Esau and Israel." (1 Chronicles 1:34) Israel is the name this book uses for Isaac's second son. The list lines up Esau's family first, so keep your eyes open.

Shem and Japheth are two of Noah's sons (1 Chronicles 1:4), so they're many generations before Isaac. Isaac's sons are named here: "Esau and Israel." (1 Chronicles 1:34) Mixing up two brothers from one family tree with two from another is easy when the whole chapter is names.

Nebaioth and Kedar are sons of Ishmael (1 Chronicles 1:29), and Ishmael is Isaac's brother. That makes them Isaac's nephews, not his sons. The verse says: "The sons of Isaac: Esau and Israel." (1 Chronicles 1:34) Close family, wrong branch.

Right on. The verse says: "These are the kings who reigned in the land of Edom before any king reigned over the Israelites." (1 Chronicles 1:43) Edom had kings first. The book just lays that out and keeps walking.

The Egyptians are a real nation in the Bible, but they're not the ones in this verse. It says Edom's kings reigned "before any king reigned over the Israelites." (1 Chronicles 1:43) So the comparison is with Israel, not Egypt. Nice try, friend.

The Philistines do show up earlier in this chapter. They're said to have come from the Casluhites (1 Chronicles 1:12). But this verse is about someone else: Edom's kings reigned "before any king reigned over the Israelites." (1 Chronicles 1:43) So Israelites is the answer. I'd say you got lost in the family tree, and I've done that myself.
